title: Pehle Tirthankara ne 400 din bhookha kyun raha?
hooks: Pehle Tirthankara ne 400 din bhookha kyun raha?
400 din tak kisi ne nahi diya pehla ahara — kyun?
Rishabhanatha ne 400 din intezaar kiya, phir kya hua?
hook_why: Named entity (Rishabhanatha) + specific number (400 din) + question in first 6 words — matches raaz hook rule and Jain katha hook style.
metaphor: Golden sugarcane juice flowing into a monk's cupped hands — the first correct alms after a year of wrong offerings.
mechanism: Rishabhanatha chhoda raj-paat, bane pehle sadhu — logon ko pata nahi tha ahara ka niyam.
Gaonwale sona, ghode, betiyan le aaye — muni ne kuch nahi liya, sirf shuddh bhav se diya hua anna sweekar karte hain.
400 din beet gaye, Akshaya Tritiya pe Raja Shreyansa ko pichhle janam ki yaad aayi.
Unhone ikshu-ras (ganne ka ras) swarna ke bartan mein, prem se bhent kiya — yeh pehla sahi ahara tha.
Tabse Jain parampara mein ahara-vidhi ka niyam shuru hua: daan dena kaafi nahi, sahi tarika aur bhav bhi chahiye.

claims.claim: Rishabhanatha (Adinatha) is the first Tirthankara of the present half-cycle in Jain cosmology.
claims.basis: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra by Hemachandra; Adipurana by Jinasena; Wikipedia Rishabhanatha page.

claims.claim: After renunciation, Rishabhanatha wandered without food for 400 days because people did not know the correct method of offering alms (ahara) to a monk.
claims.basis: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra (as cited in Wikipedia); Adipurana; Jain tradition.

claims.claim: On Akshaya Tritiya, King Shreyansa offered sugarcane juice (ikshu rasa) in golden vessels, which became the first correct alms accepted by Rishabhanatha.
claims.basis: Trishashti-shalaka-purusha-charitra; Adipurana; standard Jain narrative of Akshaya Tritiya origin.

claims.claim: This event established the tradition of ahara (alms-giving) for Jain monks, which continues today with specific rules.
claims.basis: Jain monastic practice documented in Agamas and living tradition.

fresh_fixed: <scene 1: The script claims a 365-day fast, but the Wikipedia source (citing Trishashti-Shalakapurusha-Charitra) states Rishabhanatha traveled without food for 400 days.>
